_readme: Golden-prompt corpus: real teacher asks and what the Create flow should
resolve each one to. Two consumers:
EXPECTED DELIVERABLE is deliverable today — the game validates, the
recipe compiles clean, the reference storyboard compiles from real
bricks. It does NOT call any AI.
2. scripts/eval-designer-prompts.js (manual, real AI): runs each prompt
through the live matcher and diffs what it chose against 'expect'.
Run it before AND after touching a matcher/storyboard prompt.
Kinds: host (a built-in game), recipe (id + params merged over defaults),
storyboard (a reference brick realization), cantBuild (documented honest
gap — the platform should say no, not fake it).

prompts.prompt: Students build sentences together, but each student adds only ONE word and cannot see any of the words written before theirs. At the end everyone sees the surprise sentence they started, finished by classmates.
Each student starts a story and passes it on. The next writer can only see the last few words of what came before, adds a line, and passes again. At the end the whole stories are revealed.
prompts.note: Nearest current match; a dedicated folded-story recipe on collect.showTail is the natural follow-on. story-builder is a defensible pick (same chain, no fold).

prompts.prompt: A fast-paced quiz with points for speed and a leaderboard at the end. I have my own multiple choice questions.
An icebreaker where each student writes two true statements and one lie about themselves and the class guesses which one is the lie.
Everyone answers one big question alone first, then pairs combine their answers into one stronger answer that the whole class sees.
A story that grows as it passes from student to student, each one adding to it, and at the end every story returns to the student who started it.
For review: students list what they remember from today's lesson from memory, then classmates add things the list missed, and it comes back to its author.
Students guess a number, like how many jelly beans are in the jar or how long the Amazon river is, and we see whose guess was closest.
Students draw a picture of a phrase, then everyone writes fake captions for each other's drawings and tries to spot the real one.
Each student writes a riddle about one of our vocabulary words, then the class sees each riddle and guesses the word.

storyboard.name: Vocab Riddles
storyboard.description: Write a riddle for a vocabulary word, then guess everyone else's.

steps.text: Pick one of our vocabulary words and keep it secret. You are going to write a riddle about it!
Your word and your riddle.
steps.clueLabel: Your riddle (no fair using the word!)

steps.text: Every word earned, every riddle solved. Nice work, wordsmiths.

prompts.note: KNOWN MISS 2026-08-30 baseline: the matcher picked recipe:creative-vote instead of handing off (noMatch) — it fakes a weak fit rather than letting the storyboard generator build the guessing-rounds shape. Matcher-prompt finding, parked.

prompts.prompt: Everyone rates their stress on a scale of 1 to 10, then predicts what the class average will be, and we see how close the predictions were.

storyboard.name: Guess the Class
storyboard.description: Rate yourself on a scale, then predict the class average.

steps.text: Two numbers coming up: first how YOU feel, then a prediction about the whole class.
On a scale of 1 to 10, how stressed are you feeling right now?
Now predict: what do you think the class average stress level will be, from 1 to 10?
That is the class, and that is how well you read it.

prompts.note: Owner built this on the live site 2026-09-12 and got a bare number box with no bounds; the estimate brick now carries min and max for a scale question, and the runtime reads the wording when it is missing (engine/phases/estimate-range.js).

prompts.prompt: Each student writes a hypothesis about tomorrow's egg drop experiment. It passes to a classmate who adds one piece of supporting evidence or reasoning, then to another classmate who adds a counterargument. At the end everyone sees what happened to the hypothesis they wrote.

storyboard.name: Hypothesis Relay
storyboard.description: A hypothesis travels: one classmate argues for it, another argues against, then it comes home.

steps.text: Science court is in session. You will write a hypothesis about tomorrow's egg drop, and two classmates will put it on trial.

steps.start: Write one hypothesis about tomorrow's egg drop experiment. What will happen, and to which design?
hops: Read the hypothesis above. Add ONE piece of supporting evidence or reasoning below it.
Read the hypothesis and the evidence above. Add ONE counterargument or complication below them.

steps.text: Every hypothesis got a defender and a skeptic. Tomorrow, the eggs decide.

prompts.note: The chain-brick case: per-hop instructions differ, so no fixed recipe covers it. idea-chain is a defensible near-match.

prompts.prompt: An activity where everyone shares what they're most afraid of and then you have to guess who shared what. And then afterwards you see everyone's answer and you collectively rank them in order of how scary you think they are.

storyboard.name: Fear Factor
storyboard.description: Share a fear, guess whose it is, then rank them together from scariest down.

steps.text: Everyone shares one thing they are afraid of. Then we find out how well we know each other: each fear goes up, and the class guesses whose it is.
What are you most afraid of? One honest line.
Every fear the class shared:
Put these in order, scariest at the top.
Brave room. Everyone is afraid of something, and now we know a little more about each other.

prompts.note: The prompt that found the dead storyboard door (2026-09-07). Needs guess:who on guessing-rounds (the typed-guess default guesses the secret) and the rank brick (a vote is not a ranking). Who Said It? covers the first half only.

prompts.prompt: writing prompt generator, the class everyone lists 4 people and 4 circumstances then they are shuffled and everyone gets one person and one circumstance.

storyboard.name: Prompt Generator
storyboard.description: Everyone adds a person and a circumstance, the piles are shuffled and dealt, and each student writes from the pair they drew.

steps.text: We are building writing prompts together. You will add a person and a circumstance to the piles. Then the piles get shuffled and you will be dealt one of each, invented by classmates, to write from.

piles.label: A person
piles.prompt: Name a person a story could be about. A lighthouse keeper, a substitute teacher on their first day, a retired spy who misses the work...

piles.label: A circumstance
piles.prompt: Name a circumstance, something happening or about to happen. Stuck in an elevator, the last day of summer, a power cut in the middle of an exam...

steps.text: Write the opening paragraph of a story that puts your person in your circumstance.
Every prompt in this room was built by three people. Keep yours, it is the start of something.

prompts.note: The shuffle-and-deal prompt (2026-09-07). Story Ingredients is the same mechanic with three fixed piles, a fine host answer; the deal brick lets the storyboard build it with the teacher's own piles.

prompts.prompt: I just want to ask the class one question and see everyone's answers on the board.

params.question: What is one thing you learned today?

prompts.prompt: Students record a two minute podcast segment about the chapter and we listen to them together.

expect.reason: No audio or video recording; the platform is text and simple taps.

prompts.prompt: My students are in teams. Each team picks a first and second choice among four categories (self and identity, working with others, thinking and problem solving, execution and adaptation). Each group decides on its top choices, and then the categories are assigned to the groups.
prompts.note: The owner's prompt (2026-09-16), which the storyboard could not build before the assign brick and the Choice Draft recipe existed.

prompts.prompt: Split the class into groups of three. Each group ranks the six chapter topics they would rather present, then give every group one topic so no more than two groups share a chapter. Finish by showing who got what.

storyboard.name: Chapter Draft
storyboard.description: Groups rank the chapters, then each is handed one.

steps.text: Time to divide up the chapters. Your group ranks the six chapters, favorite on top, and the draft hands each group one.
Which chapter would your group rather present? First choice at the top.
Here is who presents what.
Chapters are set. Start planning with your group.

prompts.note: The same shape with a teacher's own list and a cap per item: teams, rank as groups, assign (2026-09-16).

prompts.prompt: Debate pairs: partners get opposite sides of a question, write an opening argument, swap with their partner, write a rebuttal, then switch and argue the other side.

storyboard.name: Debate Pairs
storyboard.description: Partners argue opposite sides of one question, rebut each other, then switch.

steps.text: You and a partner will take opposite sides of one question. Argue yours, answer theirs, then trade places.
Should homework be banned? You are arguing {{side}}. Write your opening argument.
rounds: Read your partner's opening below. Write a rebuttal, still arguing {{side}}.
Switch sides: you now argue {{otherSide}}. Answer your partner's rebuttal below from that side.

steps.text: You argued both sides. Which one was harder to make?

prompts.note: The pairs-brick case (storyboard probe, 2026-09-20): the one idea a teacher got nothing for. Partners, rounds with the partner's piece in view, sides dealt and switched.

prompts.prompt: Watch this YouTube clip https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ then answer two questions about it.

storyboard.name: Clip and Two Questions
storyboard.description: The class watches a clip on the projector, then answers two questions about it.

steps.text: Eyes up front. We are watching a short clip together, then you will answer two questions about it on your device.
In one sentence, what was the clip mostly about?
Here is what the class took from it:
What is one question the clip left you with?
The questions we still have:
Good watching. We will pick up those questions next time.

prompts.note: The video case (storyboard probe, 2026-09-20): the other idea a teacher got nothing for. The clip rides on the announce brick's video field and plays on the projector.

prompts.prompt: Groups of four, each member gets a job (Facilitator, Recorder, Timekeeper, Reporter), then the group works through a shared to-do list for the lab.

storyboard.name: Lab Jobs
storyboard.description: Groups of four, a job for every member, then one shared lab checklist per group.

steps.text: Lab day. You will be put in groups of four, every one of you gets a job, and your group works through today's list together.
Work through the lab with your group. Tagged tasks belong to a job, but everyone backs each other up.
tasks: Set up your station and check the materials
Timekeeper: call out the halfway point
Facilitator: make sure everyone has done a step
Clean up and return the materials

steps.text: Reporters, get ready to share what your group found.

prompts.note: The roles-brick case (storyboard probe, 2026-09-20): jobs per member had compiled to teams > rank > assign, which hands one job per GROUP. Group Work Day is the matcher's defensible answer.

prompts.prompt: Guess how many times the average heart beats in a day. Closest guess wins.

storyboard.name: Heartbeat Guess
storyboard.description: One number to estimate, the closest guess takes the points.

steps.text: One question, one number. Reason it out, lock in your guess, and the closest guess takes the points.
How many times does the average human heart beat in one day?
About a hundred thousand. Your heart did a few dozen of those while you guessed.

prompts.note: The estimate-answer case (storyboard probe, 2026-09-20): with an answer the estimate step reveals the number, the class spread, and closeness scores; without one it is a poll and no text may promise a winner. Estimation Station is the matcher's defensible answer.

prompts.prompt: Draw a monster, put all the drawings on the wall, and vote for the scariest one.

storyboard.name: Monster Wall
storyboard.description: Everyone draws a monster; after the teacher's look, the wall opens one drawing at a time, then the class votes for the scariest and the winner goes up under the crown.

steps.text: Ninety seconds to draw the scariest monster you can. Every drawing goes up on the wall, then you vote for the one that gives you chills.
Draw a monster. Scary, silly, or both, but make it yours.
steps.gallery: The monster wall is open. Look closely, you will be voting in a moment.

steps.text: That was the monster wall. Sleep well.

prompts.note: The draw-brick case (storyboard probe, 2026-09-20): declined 3 of 3 as typed-text-only while Draw Gallery did it. Since the vote over drawings (the same night) the ballot shows thumbnails and the crown shows the winning drawing. Draw Gallery is the matcher's defensible answer.

prompts.prompt: Everyone answers one question, then the answers get summed up into three themes for the board.

storyboard.name: Three Themes
storyboard.description: One open question, every answer read, three themes on the board to talk through.

steps.text: One question, everyone answers, and we will see the three big things this room is thinking.
What is one thing about this unit that still feels confusing?
Group the answers into exactly three themes. Give each theme a short plain heading and quote one answer under it, no names.
steps.heading: The three things this class is saying:

steps.text: Pick one theme and we will start there next time.

prompts.note: The summarize-brick case (storyboard probe, 2026-09-20): declined 3 of 3 while ai-process summarize had done it since the start. Discussion Starter is the matcher's defensible answer. The heading never names the AI.

prompts.prompt: Everyone draws a picture of me and then we vote on which one is the best.

storyboard.name: Portraits of the Teacher
storyboard.description: Everyone draws the teacher, the wall opens after a quick look, and the class votes for the best one.

steps.text: Ninety seconds to draw me. Be kind, or be funny, but be quick. Then the wall opens and you vote for the best one.
Draw a picture of your teacher.
steps.gallery: The portrait wall is open. Look closely, you vote next.

steps.text: Thank you, I think. The winner goes on the fridge.

prompts.note: The owner's own live try (2026-09-21): the matcher sent it to Creative Vote (a text box) once and Draw Gallery (no vote) twice; every recipe's answer box is typed, so a drawing idea with a vote is the step builder's (draw then vote). No acceptAlso: the vote is the heart, so Draw Gallery is not a defensible answer here.

prompts.prompt: A five-minute anonymous poll for my history class: what was the main cause of the American Revolution? The choices are taxation without representation, the Proclamation of 1763, the Boston Massacre, and Enlightenment ideas. Show the results, then we discuss.

params.question: What was the main cause of the American Revolution?

prompts.note: A reviewer's try (2026-09-23): the matcher answered with the Live Poll built-in ("Good news: this already exists") and Make it yours opened the default question about today's lesson, names Shown. The built-in is the live-poll recipe with its defaults, so the answer is the recipe with the teacher's question and all four of their choices; the route refits a recipe-born pick to its recipe as the net, and reads "anonymous" itself. No host: answer: the whole point is the content traveling.

prompts.prompt: Constitutional Convention: each student secretly gets a state, writes one clause their state needs, and the class votes clauses into a constitution that grows on the projector.

storyboard.name: Constitutional Convention
storyboard.description: Every delegate gets a state in secret, writes one clause, and the class votes.

steps.text: Welcome, delegates. Each of you represents one state. Nobody else knows which, so speak for your state, not yourself.
You represent {{thisStep.assigned}}. Write one clause your state needs in the constitution.
Which clause belongs in our constitution?
The convention is adjourned. Every state spoke, and the clause with the most votes leads our constitution.

prompts.note: An outside reviewer's try (2026-09-24): the storyboard reached for rank then assign, which lists every student's state on the projector, and the results step read {{vote.winner}}, a player id. The collect brick's items deal the states in private ({{thisStep.assigned}} on each student's screen, a blank on the projector), the vote brick appends the crown, and a vote's .winner in a step's words is rewritten to .winnerText.

prompts.prompt: I ask review questions out loud, the first student to buzz in answers, and I mark it right or wrong. Wrong answers lock you out until the next question.

storyboard.name: Buzzer Round
storyboard.description: The teacher asks out loud, the first to buzz answers.

steps.text: Review time. I will ask the questions out loud. Buzz fast, answer faster; a wrong answer sits you out until the next one.
Listen for the question, then buzz!
That is the round. Nice reflexes.

prompts.note: A reviewer's routine (2026-09-27): the matcher called a buzzer "off screen" and the storyboard had no buzz brick, while the buzz step type ran Lightning Round all along.

prompts.prompt: Hot seat: students submit questions for the student in the hot seat, I pick which ones go up on the board one at a time.

storyboard.name: Hot Seat
storyboard.description: Students write questions, the teacher picks which go up.

steps.text: One of us is in the hot seat. Write a question you would like them to answer; I will pick the ones we use.
Your question for the hot seat.
The questions for the hot seat:
Out of the hot seat. Thanks for the questions.

prompts.note: A reviewer's routine (2026-09-27): the review brick is the teacher gate (preview) plus a one-at-a-time reveal; the plan used to refuse it.

prompts.prompt: Should zoos exist, yes or no? Then pair each student with someone who answered differently to trade reasons, then vote again.

storyboard.name: Zoo Debate
storyboard.description: Pick a side, argue it with someone who picked the other, vote again.

steps.text: Should zoos exist?
You and your partner chose differently. Give them your strongest reason.
rounds: Read your partner's reason below. What is the best answer to it?

steps.text: After hearing the other side: should zoos exist?
Minds may have moved. That is what the trade was for.

prompts.note: A reviewer's routine (2026-09-27): the matcher sent it to Both Sides of the Rope and dropped the opposite pairing; the pairs brick carries pairBy now (the engine's answer-keyed pairing).

prompts.prompt: Jigsaw: split into four expert groups, each reads one section and writes the key ideas, then regroup so every new group has one expert from each section and they teach each other.

storyboard.name: Jigsaw Reading
storyboard.description: Expert groups become home groups.

steps.text: Four sections, four expert groups. Learn yours well: you will be the only one who read it in your next group.
Write the three key ideas of your section in your own words.
New groups: one expert from each section. Teach your section, then listen to the other three.
Four sections, every one of you now knows all four.

prompts.note: A reviewer's routine (2026-09-27): the regroup is a team-split with method jigsaw (engine/phases/team-grouping.js jigsawGroups), one member of each earlier group per new group.

prompts.prompt: March Madness for our next read-aloud: eight books in a bracket, the class votes each matchup, winners advance until one book is left.

storyboard.name: Book Bracket
storyboard.description: Eight books, three rounds, one read-aloud.

steps.text: Eight books walk in, one walks out. Vote every matchup; the winners meet in the next round.
Which book should we read next?
We have our next read-aloud. Grab a spot on the rug.

prompts.note: A reviewer's routine (2026-09-27): the matcher forced it into Elimination Tournament (answers voted down each round), whose params failed, and the teacher saw an internal line; the bracket brick chains head-to-head votes with bracket: true, the winners moving on.

prompts.prompt: Fist to five on how well they understand fractions, then pair the 0s, 1s, and 2s with the 4s and 5s so the confident ones explain it to a partner who is not.

storyboard.name: Fist to Five
storyboard.description: Rate yourself, then the sure explain to the unsure.

steps.text: Fist to five: how well do you understand fractions right now?
One of you is surer than the other. The surer one: explain fractions in your own words. The other: ask what is still fuzzy.
A fist can become a five. Nice work, both of you.

prompts.note: A reviewer's second pass (2026-09-28): the plan used pairBy "opposite", which only means the answers differ, so a 4 sat with a 5. "far" pairs the ends of the scale together.

prompts.prompt: Anonymous question box: everyone types a question they were afraid to ask, the class upvotes, and the top five go on the board.

storyboard.name: Question Box
storyboard.description: Ask what you were afraid to ask; the top five go up.

steps.text: No names on these. Ask the thing you have been wondering.
What is one question you have not asked yet?
Five questions the class wanted answered. We start there tomorrow.

prompts.note: A reviewer's second pass (2026-09-28): the built version listed "Did not pass" with counts under students' own questions and had no top-five limit; showRejected: false and top: 5 on the vote brick.

prompts.prompt: A quick mood check at the start of class

params.question: How are you feeling as class starts?

prompts.prompt: Spanish 1 vocabulary review: match the color words to their English meanings
Each student ranks the five causes of World War I from most to least important, then we see the class order

storyboard.name: Causes of World War I
storyboard.description: Every student puts the five causes in order; the class order goes up.

steps.text: Five causes of World War I. Put them in order, most important at the top, then we see the class's order.
Most important cause at the top.
Where did your order differ from the class? Be ready to defend your top pick.

prompts.prompt: Jigsaw: three fixed expert groups each answer a question about their section, then share with a group that has one person from each

storyboard.name: Expert Groups
storyboard.description: Three expert groups answer about their section, then regroup to teach it.

steps.text: Three sections, three expert groups. Answer the question about your section together; you will teach it in your next group.
What are the three most important ideas in your section?
New groups: one expert from each section. Teach yours, then listen to the other two.
Every one of you now knows all three sections.

prompts.prompt: Peer feedback on each other's thesis statements: every student gets feedback from a classmate on their own thesis

storyboard.name: Thesis Check
storyboard.description: Write a thesis, a classmate gives feedback, and it comes back to you.

steps.text: Write your thesis, then a classmate reads it and leaves you feedback. It comes back to you at the end.

steps.draft: Write your thesis statement in one or two sentences.
steps.text: Read your classmate's thesis below. Write one strength and one question for the writer.
Read the feedback on your thesis and revise one sentence before you leave.

prompts.prompt: Match five dates to the events of the French Revolution, then sort eight statements about it into Fact or Opinion, both scored, with the standings at the end.

storyboard.name: Revolution Review
storyboard.description: Match the dates, sort the statements, see the standings.

steps.text: Two rounds on the French Revolution: match the dates, then sort the statements. Both count.
Match each date to its event.
Fact or opinion?

items.text: The Terror was the worst part of the Revolution

steps.text: That is the review. Nice work.

prompts.note: Two graded bricks in a row share one standings step (2026-09-30, the mechanics inventory): match and sort existed as steps for months with no brick.

prompts.prompt: After each student presents, the class rates the presentation on clarity and creativity from 1 to 5, but only I see the results; then everyone writes one suggestion for the presenter.

storyboard.name: Presentation Feedback
storyboard.description: Rate the presentation on two scales, then one suggestion each.

steps.text: As each presenter finishes, rate them honestly. Only your teacher sees the scores.
Rate the presentation.
One suggestion for the presenter.
Thank you, presenters.

prompts.note: rate with results to the teacher only; the rate step had no brick.

prompts.prompt: Students take a five-question quiz on fractions at their own pace on their own devices, no timer and no winners, then write one question they still have, and I pick which questions to go over on the board.

storyboard.name: Fractions Check
storyboard.description: A self-paced quiz, then the questions you still have.

steps.text: Work through the quiz at your own pace. When you finish, tell me what is still fuzzy.
Fractions check
One thing about fractions that is still fuzzy.
The questions we will go over:
Good work. See you tomorrow.

prompts.note: solo-quiz as a brick (no standings unless asked), then review.

prompts.prompt: Before I reveal the result of the experiment, everyone bets points on which of three predictions will come true: the ice melts first, the salt water freezes first, or they tie. Then I announce the winner and we see who bet right.

storyboard.name: Place Your Bets
storyboard.description: Bet on the outcome, then see who called it.

steps.text: Three predictions on the board. Bet your points on the one you believe.
Which prediction comes true?
Science does not care what we bet. Nice calls, everyone.

prompts.note: wager with no known answer: the teacher picks the winner on the console; the standings follow.

prompts.prompt: Everyone writes their own definition of democracy, then pairs combine their two into one, then two pairs combine into one, and the class sees the final definitions on the board.

storyboard.name: Democracy, Defined Together
storyboard.description: Alone, then pairs, then fours, one definition each.

steps.text: First on your own, then with a partner, then with another pair. One definition survives each round.
Define democracy in one sentence.
Combine your two definitions into one stronger one.
steps.heading: The definitions the fours built:

steps.text: Four definitions, built by all of us.

prompts.note: merge with groupSize 4 builds two merge steps (pairs, then fours) and the reveal; the merge step had no brick.

prompts.prompt: We write a class poem about autumn, one line per student, each one adding the next line on their turn with 30 seconds to write, then we read the whole poem on the board.

storyboard.name: Autumn, Line by Line
storyboard.description: One line each, in turn, into one class poem.

steps.text: One poem, one line each. When it is your turn, read what came before and add the next line.
Add the next line of our autumn poem.
steps.heading: Our autumn poem:

steps.text: Read it aloud together, slowly.

prompts.note: relay as a brick: a turn each, the finished piece revealed after.

prompts.prompt: Lab day: groups of three work through a six-step checklist (gather materials, measure the water, record the temperature every minute, graph it, clean up, submit the sheet) while I watch every group's progress on the board.

storyboard.name: Lab Day
storyboard.description: Groups of three through six steps, progress on the board.

steps.text: Six steps, one group. Tick each one off as you finish it; I can see where every group is.
Work through the lab together.
Sheets in. Nice lab.

prompts.note: tasks as a brick over the last teams step; the checklist had no brick of its own.

prompts.prompt: Joke-off: everyone writes a joke, the class votes, the bottom half are out, the survivors write a new joke, and it repeats until one comedian is left.

storyboard.name: Joke-Off
storyboard.description: Write, vote, half are out, repeat until one is left.

steps.text: Every round: write a joke, vote for the funniest (not your own), and the bottom half are out. Last comedian standing wins.
Your best joke. Keep it clean.
Take a bow.

prompts.note: knockout builds the Elimination Tournament loop from one brick.

prompts.prompt: Charades in two teams: everyone writes a movie title, then the teams take turns acting them out, one actor at a time, 60 seconds a turn, with points for each one guessed.

storyboard.name: Movie Charades
storyboard.description: Your movie titles, acted out by team.

steps.text: Write a movie title the whole class would know. Then teams take turns acting them out.
Act it out, no words! Your team guesses.
steps.phrases: Write a movie title everyone would know.

steps.text: And the award goes to all of you.

prompts.note: charades builds the teams and the phrase step when the plan has neither; team standings after.

prompts.prompt: A focus warm-up: the class counts to 30 together, anyone can say the next number, but if two people go at the same time we start over from zero.

storyboard.name: Thirty as One
storyboard.description: Count to thirty, one voice at a time.

steps.text: Thirty, as one voice. Anyone can tap the next number; two at once and we start over.
Listen more, rush less. That was the lesson.

prompts.note: count as a brick over the one-voice step, the summary after built in.

prompts.prompt: As students finish the test they answer two things on their own: how confident do they feel from 1 to 5, and one thing that confused them. No waiting for the rest of the class.

storyboard.name: Confidence Ticket
storyboard.description: Two questions as each student finishes.

steps.text: How confident do you feel about today's test?
One thing that confused you.
Thanks. Put your device away.

prompts.note: rolling: true at the top of the plan: students start as they join; the compiler drops timers and refuses roster-bound steps.

prompts.prompt: Everyone picks a side on "Should homework be banned?" (yes, no, not sure), then I want everyone who picked the same answer together in groups of four to build their side's best argument, and then each group reads it out.

storyboard.name: Pick a Side, Build a Case
storyboard.description: Pick a side, group with your side, build the argument.

steps.text: Pick a side first. Then you will sit with everyone who picked the same side and build your best argument together.
Should homework be banned?
Find your group on the board. Build your side's best argument in three sentences; one of you will read it out.
Every side had its say.

prompts.note: teams groupBy "same" (2026-09-30): team-split method byAnswer over the last pick-one step, a group size splitting a big answer.

prompts.prompt: A secret-role game: everyone is privately handed a role, two are spies and the rest are crew. Everyone writes one sentence about what the crew should do next, we read them, then the class votes on who they think is a spy, and the most-voted student is out of the round.

storyboard.name: Spies Among the Crew
storyboard.description: Secret roles, one sentence each, then vote a suspect out.

steps.text: Your role is private. Spies, blend in. Crew, watch for anything odd.

You are: {{thisStep.assigned}}

Write one sentence about what the crew should do next.
items: Spy: you are one of two. Blend in and sound helpful.
Spy: you are one of two. Blend in and sound helpful.
Crew: find the spies by what they write.
Crew: find the spies by what they write.
Crew: find the spies by what they write.
Crew: find the spies by what they write.

steps.text: Read every sentence. Who sounds like a spy?
Who do you think is a spy?
One suspect is out. Were you right? Spies, reveal yourselves.

prompts.note: vote over "students" with out: true (2026-09-30): candidates "players", excludeAuthors, then eliminate most-votes. Secret roles are fine; nobody is killed, they are out of the round.

prompts.prompt: Students put six events of the American Revolution in the right order on their devices: Boston Tea Party, Lexington and Concord, Declaration of Independence, Saratoga, Yorktown, Treaty of Paris. Points for each event in the right slot, then we see the right order and the standings.

storyboard.name: Revolution in Order
storyboard.description: Put six events in order; points per right slot.

steps.text: Six events, scrambled. Drag them into the order they happened. Every event in its right slot scores.
Put the events in the order they happened, earliest at the top.
That is the order. Now you know the story.

prompts.note: rank correct: true (2026-09-30): the items in their right order become correctOrder, the step shows them shuffled, the reveal shows both orders, the standings follow.

prompts.prompt: Each student writes one quiz question about the water cycle with the right answer and two wrong ones, then the whole class takes the quiz made of everyone's questions at their own pace.

storyboard.name: The Water Cycle, Quizzed by Us
storyboard.description: You write the questions, then everyone takes the quiz.

steps.text: You are writing the quiz today. One question each, a right answer, and two wrong ones that could fool a classmate.
Write one question about the water cycle.
steps.title: The water cycle, by us

steps.text: A quiz written by the class, taken by the class.

prompts.note: write-quiz (2026-09-30): a keyed collect (question, correct, wrong1, wrong2) then solo-quiz questionsFrom.

prompts.prompt: Everyone types one word that describes how they feel about the exam, and we see a word cloud on the board where the words more of us typed are bigger.

storyboard.name: One Word Before the Exam
storyboard.description: One word each, then a word cloud of the class.

steps.text: One word. How do you feel about the exam? The more of us who pick a word, the bigger it gets.
One word that describes how you feel about the exam.
How we feel, in our own words:
Now we know where we all are.

prompts.note: reveal style "cloud" (2026-09-30): {{ask.responses.cloud}}, drawn sized by the screens.

prompts.prompt: Everyone writes their best idea for the fundraiser, we see them all up on the board at once, and then a random student is drawn to present theirs first.

storyboard.name: Fundraiser Ideas
storyboard.description: Every idea up at once, then a random presenter.

steps.text: Your best fundraiser idea, in a sentence. They all go up at once, then one of you is drawn to go first.
Your best idea for the fundraiser.
Every idea, all at once:
Drawn to present first: {{players.random}}. Tell us about yours.
Great ideas. We vote next week.

prompts.note: reveal style "cards" and {{players.random}} (2026-09-30): every answer as a card, then a fair random draw of a student.

prompts.prompt: From a list of six causes of World War I, each student picks up to three they think mattered most, and we see the tally on the board.

storyboard.name: Three Causes
storyboard.description: Pick up to three causes, see the class tally.

steps.text: Six causes on the board. Pick up to three you think mattered most.
Which causes mattered most? Pick up to three.
Now we argue about the top ones.

prompts.note: collect-choice maxPicks (2026-09-30): several picks on one ballot, every pick counted; the poll results reveal follows by the poll rule.

prompts.prompt: A quick fill-in-the-blank: "The powerhouse of the cell is the ____." Students type the answer, it is marked right or wrong automatically, and the standings go up.

storyboard.name: Fill the Blank
storyboard.description: Type the missing word; marked at once.

steps.text: One blank, one word. Type it and send it; the answer is marked when I close the question.
The powerhouse of the cell is the ____.
The answer was {{ask.correctAnswer}}. {{ask.correctCount}} of {{ask.answeredCount}} had it.
Nice. On to the next organelle.

prompts.note: collect answer + accepted (2026-09-30): a graded open answer by normalized match, the standings built in.

prompts.prompt: Lab stations: split the class into four groups, and each group gets a different task on their screens (measure the water, graph the readings, label the diagram, write the conclusion), then each group reports back in one sentence.

storyboard.name: Four Stations
storyboard.description: Four groups, four tasks, one report each.

steps.text: Four stations, four groups. Your screen tells you your station's task.
Your station: {{thisStep.station}}
stations: Measure the water and record the temperature every minute.
Graph the readings from the measuring station.
Label the diagram of the setup.
Write the conclusion in two sentences.

steps.text: Report back: what did your group find or make?
What every station found:
Four stations, one lab. Well done.

prompts.note: stations on an announce (2026-09-30): a line per group where {{thisStep.station}} stands, bound to the step's id by the compiler.

prompts.prompt: Students write a short paragraph explaining the causes of the Dust Bowl. Then two different classmates each read it and leave a glow and a grow, without seeing each other's comments, and the writer gets both back.

storyboard.name: Glow and Grow
storyboard.description: Two classmates read your Dust Bowl paragraph and each leave a glow and a grow.

steps.text: In a short paragraph, explain the causes of the Dust Bowl.
Read your classmate's paragraph below. Write one glow (something that works) and one grow (one thing to make clearer).
Read your two comments and revise one sentence of your paragraph.

prompts.prompt: Give my class two minutes of silent thinking about whether the Constitution should be easier to amend, then they turn and talk with a partner, then everyone votes yes or no.

storyboard.name: Think, Talk, Vote
storyboard.description: Two quiet minutes, a partner talk, then a class vote on amending the Constitution.

steps.text: Should the Constitution be easier to amend? Think it over quietly: one reason for, one reason against.
steps.talk: Turn to a partner and share which reason convinced you more.

steps.text: Should the Constitution be easier to amend?
Thanks for thinking it through.

prompts.prompt: A four-question review quiz on the water cycle where students also say how sure they are of each answer, so we can talk about being certain and wrong.

storyboard.name: Sure About the Water Cycle?
storyboard.description: Four water cycle questions, each followed by how sure you were.

questions.text: What is it called when water vapor turns into liquid?
Rain, snow, and hail are all forms of what?
Water given off by plants is called what?

steps.text: Which answer were you most sure of and wrong about? Talk it over.

prompts.prompt: Let my class pick our next novel from five choices with ranked-choice voting: everyone ranks them and we use instant runoff so the winner has a majority.

storyboard.name: Pick Our Next Novel
storyboard.description: Everyone ranks five novels and instant runoff picks the one the class wants most.

steps.text: Rank all five novels, your favorite at the top. If your first pick goes out, your vote moves to your next choice.
Put these novels in order, the one you most want to read at the top.
That is our next novel.

prompts.prompt: Hot seat for our novel: a student plays Brian from Hatchet, the class writes questions for him, I check them first, and they go to that student one at a time to answer in character.

storyboard.name: Brian in the Hot Seat
storyboard.description: The class questions Brian from Hatchet, played by one student.

steps.text: One of you will become Brian from Hatchet. Everyone else, get ready to ask him anything.
Write one question for Brian about his time in the wilderness.
steps.heading: Brian, the class asks:

steps.text: Thank you, Brian. What surprised you about his answers?

prompts.prompt: Find your match: each student secretly gets either a vocabulary word or its definition from our cell biology unit, they walk around to find their partner, and we see who found each other.

storyboard.name: Cell Word Match
storyboard.description: Each of you holds a word or its meaning; find the classmate with the other half.

steps.text: You will get a card with a word or a meaning. Get up and find the classmate whose card goes with yours.
Find the classmate whose card goes with yours, then tap their name.

pairs.right: Controls what goes in and out

steps.text: Which pair was hardest to find, and why?

prompts.prompt: Geography estimation: how many square kilometers is Yemen, how tall is Mount Everest, how long is the Nile. Points based on how close you are, and a speed bonus.

storyboard.name: How Close Can You Get?
storyboard.description: Three geography guesses, points for how close and how fast.

steps.text: How many square kilometers is Yemen?
How tall is Mount Everest, in meters?
How long is the Nile, in kilometers?
Which guess surprised you most?
